newsitem.title: LEBANON: Troops deployed in Beirut on eve of protest.
newsitem.headline: Troops deployed in Beirut on eve of protest.

text.p: Lebanese troops began deploying in Beirut on Wednesday ready to prevent planned anti-government demonstrations on Thursday, witnesses said.
A Reuters reporter saw troops in armoured personnel carriers deploying in west Beirut's Hamra commercial district.
Truckloads of troops drove past the Reuters office in the city and other units were seen in other parts of the capital.

Earlier, Interior Minister Michel al-Murr said opposition demonstrations planned during a general strike on Thursday were banned and the army and security forces were responsible for maintaining order.
It was not clear if the army would impose a curfew on the country for the second time this year.

Murr said the army had authority to impose a curfew if necessary, as on last February 29 when it prevented similar planned demonstrations by slapping a curfew on most of the country for much of the day and arresting thousands of curfew breakers.

In February the government formally gave the army command responsibility for security and order throughout the country for six months, which included the right to impose a curfew as necessary. The government has not taken similar action this time.

"There is no curfew because the army does not have a mandate from the cabinet to take resonsibility on its own for security," a source told Reuters. The army has a strict policy of avoiding public statements and its officials declined all comment.
It was not known whether the government, tied up with a confidence debate in parliament, would meet later on Wednesday to empower the army to take over security responsibilities.
Opposition groups and labour unions have called Thursday's strike and demonstrations to protest against the media and social policies of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.
Questioned about the demonstrations by reporters, Murr said: "There is a standing decision taken by the government banning demonstrations and this decision is still valid today.
"The task of the army and security forces is to maintain security in the country and they take the measures needed for this task."
Hariri has imposed a ban on all demonstrations since 1993.
Cancellation of the ban is one of three main demands of the political groups, labour unions, students and media workers who issued the strike and demonstration call last week.

They are also protesting against the government's perceived failure to improve social conditions for most Lebanese, many of whom live below the poverty line, and against a decision to close scores of radio and television stations on Saturday.
The opposition says the way the government is applying a new law regulating the audiovisual media will muzzle the opposition and carve up the lucrative media market among its friends.
Only a handful of broadcasting licences have been granted, mostly to figures like Hariri, and all opposition stations are to close.
The pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) threw its weight behind the protests on Tuesday, raising the prospect that thousands of its supporters might take to the streets.
"Let it be a resounding cry in the face of those responsible so they may wake up from their slumber and begin to understand the extent of the suffering around them," Hizbollah said.
